name: t100_bb_stretch
headline: Human Written
windows:
Some families run on a bargain like “If I’m happy while someone I love is suffering, I’m abandoning them.”
That’s exactly why I was crying for 14 years. Beginning at the age of 12, when I really started to understand that life is brutal for most people, I became convinced that being happy myself, while others weren’t, was selfish. I had this poster in my room that really resonated with me, by the famous socialist, Eugene V.

I told this to a therapist in college and she actually agreed it was a good reason to be depressed!
What I found, once I started cultivating my own happiness, was that I got a lot better at helping other people toward theirs. That might not be how it goes for everyone, and it doesn’t mean unhappy people can’t help. Do your part for people who are suffering, and skip the part where you have to be miserable too.
Some friends or family really might not like it when you get happier, though.
Someone might pull away, or keep dragging you back into the old misery.

I’d take that loss seriously, and look at what they do and what you owe them, before deciding it’s envy.
I’d still try a small good thing, like a nice meal, and see what actually happens.

name: t100_guide_stretch
headline: Mostly Human Written
windows:
After all, sometimes “I want it NOW!” is just that: a rung on the desire treadmill. No hidden guard or old trauma required, because all creatures have endless desires naturally anyway, especially when immature. You can hear that want without shame about it. Hearing it doesn’t require giving into it, especially if getting your way would hurt you or somebody else.
I think the opposite trap can feel a lot like finally having your act together. It’s forced adulthood, and it sounds like “Nope, all good!” from somebody with a fever who’s cleaning the whole kitchen anyway. Not a lot of fun in that kitchen, and nobody gets very close to the person in it. If that’s you, clamping down harder is going to feel like the fix, but it’s just more of the same.

I’d try croaking to someone you trust, “Could you pick up some soup?” If you keep swinging between spoiling and clamping down, try staying warm while you say what happens next, like “Not now, we’ll go after lunch.”
Once a need does show, after all that hiding, it’s okay to want a lot of closeness.

So then someone you love goes for a walk alone, and you’ve texted “hello??” before they’re at the corner. When they get back, you sulk all night. Wanting them close is fine! But they get to go for a walk too.
Ask your little one what it’s afraid of.
I think it just wants to know they’re coming back.

Then the Guide can come up with something like “See you in an hour?”
The Guide doesn’t need to know everything for sure (that would be an OCD Guide, and then you’d need a Guide for the OCD Guide). It chooses the next sane step that fits your values based on the info available, and that’s how it helps your little one grow toward a whole life. Waiting to be sure first is sometimes proper & prudent, but if it’s a pattern, it can keep life on hold, and then your little one’s world stays small. Sometimes something really is stuck on someone else’s end (you’ve asked, and followed up, and there’s nothing left for you to do yet), and waiting on that isn’t avoidance.
The Guide can let it wait, keeping an eye out for when it frees up, and keep the rest of your life moving, so your little one keeps growing anyway.

Forced adulthood can get into your head too, where it wants everything as spotless as that kitchen. At your grandpa’s funeral, some dumb jingle starts up in your head and you nearly laugh during the eulogy.

That doesn’t mean you didn’t love him, or that something’s wrong with you. Minds come up with ugly and embarrassing stuff all the time, some of it the opposite of what you believe, and bodies do their own thing too.
The Guide isn’t there to police every thought.
It notices the jingle and knows you didn’t mean it, and that it isn’t who you are.
Then it goes with what you’d stand behind, which here is probably squeezing your mom’s hand and listening, and lets the jingle go.

name: t100_ended_section
headline: Human Written
windows:
When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun
Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one life ends and before the next one has formed. A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, your youngest moving out. Maybe you’ve left a family or community, maybe you’ve stayed on new terms. A therapist or helper might step back because you’re doing so much better, and suddenly your little one is wailing. For a while the old you is gone and the new you hasn’t shown up yet. Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state like that a bardo (I’m only borrowing the word, so what it teaches about death and rebirth is up to you).
Your little one might be sure everything’s over.

Usually one real thing ended, and there’s other stuff you’re still trying to keep going, maybe on autopilot. Some of it just isn’t known yet, and unknown isn’t the same as gone. Ask your little one what they’re scared will happen in the meantime (worst-case scenarios are kind of their specialty).
Something basic can mark the ending, like boxing up the old keys. Nobody needs to know what door will open next. But when the not-knowing feels too heavy, a new identity can sure look tempting. Like a borrowed coat that doesn’t fit but at least it’s warm. But you can’t go far with a borrowed coat anyway, so don’t force the future on. Keep taking care of yourself, and grieve what ended with your little one beside you during the metamorphosis.

name: t100_ifs_stretch
headline: Human Written
windows: Can’t find a calm, compassionate Self in there?

One grown-up job at a time, from a friend who’ll play Protector for a night, or from something you do, like letting the phone ring when you know how that call goes (The Parent You Inherited again), until it’s yours.
Is a perfect Higher Self already waiting in there to be your guide or parent? I’d call that claim spiritual bypassing. I’ve had the Higher Self perspective myself, though. It’s a somewhat less subjective way of seeing things as working perfectly in reality, despite the ego’s illusions, which matches what people say about it. Where I part ways with IFS is the wisdom part. I don’t think the Higher Self has any specific wisdom. It’s a vantage point, where more wisdom and compassion can come up, but problems can also look like they were never problems at all from up there, and that can ironically lead instead to more foolish indifference. You can see both sides of this see-saw in the guru types who supposedly embody their Higher Self. Anthony de Mello is an excellent example. He was a Jesuit priest who mixed stories from all kinds of traditions into his teaching on seeing through the ego’s traps and coming back to the Perfect Present. He also had a background as a psychotherapist who understood trauma-informed healing methods. He seemed to drift between the two opposite paradigms in a way that contradicted itself. And that bizarre contradiction is itself cited as “crazy wisdom” by apologists.
So inner child therapy draws on those higher vantage points more concretely. The inner Guide is the closest thing here to a Higher Self, and it has to work with the Nurturer and Protector and come after them. It can’t act like some transcendent authority that waves everything away. Most reparenting doesn’t do enough with the Guide, which is the opposite extreme from IFS, so I’m trying to bring together the best of both. IFS isn’t exactly one system, so I may be simplifying it here. It has its own branches and disputes, and that’s one more problem I’m trying to remedy by laying all this out systematically in this guide.
IFS calls these wounded young parts “exiles.” I find that pathologizing. I prefer to speak of a child who needs parenting and integration, rather than naming them by their wounded or excluded condition.
And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... At some point it’s a maze, with a little one somewhere in the middle of it.
Some practitioners are gentle about it and walk you through the maze just fine. Others seem to leave people more split up than when they started.
I wouldn’t trust a model more just because there’s a big institute behind it handing out certificates.
